## Purpose

Outlines proper maintenance and storage procedures in accordance with the factory user manual.

## Scope

Pre-deployment, post-recovery, and in-lab storage. 

::: {.callout-important}
The optode should remain shielded from ambient light when not in use to prevent bleaching of the sensing foil and preserve operational lifetime.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
The sensing foil should be wetted at least 48 hours prior to deployment or calibration. Dry sensing foil introduces a 2% sampling bias and may take several hours to equilibriate with the surrounding water.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
Swelling of the wet foil in a sample influences the response time of the optode and in turn the oxygen saturation measurement. 
:::

## Measurement Principals and Sensor Description

Oxygen optodes measure the level of oxygen saturation in a seawater sample using a method called dynamic flourescence quenching. A flourescent indicator, or luminophore, absorbs a photon from a higher energy (blue) light source and enters an excited state. After some time, the flourescent indicator will emit a lower energy (red) photon and return to its initial state. The presence of oxygen molecules, however, speeds this process up as oxygen molecuels collide with and quench the flourescent indicator.

A gas permeable sensing foil consisting of a dark optical isolation layer, flourescent indicator layer, and support layer is fixed externally over the optode's optical window. This foil is exposed to the surrounding water and allows for interaction between oxygen molecules in the sample, the indicator, and internal optics. The dark optical isolation layer prevents the influence of external light. 

As the foil is excited by modulated blue light, the optode measures the phase shift of the returned red light recieved by the photodiode. This phase shift will change depending on the presence of oxygen molecules. The optode uses a red light in conjunction with the blue light as a reference in the system. A thermistor on the optode measures the temperature of the sample. 

The optode determines the partial pressure from the measured phase shift using a series of polynomials that include the calibrated phase and temperature. The absolute oxygen concentration in μM (micromolar) is then determined as a function of the oxygen saturation that is dependent on the temperature and salinity of the sample. 


## Sensor Care

### Post-recovery

- Upon recovery, and when convenient, reapply the black rubber optode protection cap to sheild the sensor from abmbient light and prevent damage during transport. 

::: {.callout-warning}
Cleaning should be performed with caution in all cases to avoid damaging the protective foil coating and optical isolation layer.
:::

- Use a nylon brush and clean freshwater to clean the optode housing.

- Use a wet cloth to carefully clean the sensing foil.

- Calcareous fouling may be removed using a week acid (7% vinegar)

<!-- NOTE this is why we got measurements with the tape left on!!! -->
::: {.callout-note}
Unlike some traditional oxygen sensors, oxygen optodes do not consume oxygen when making a measurement. Because of this, the ability to diffuse gas has no influence on the measurement accuracy and makes oxygen optodes much more robust against fouling than traditional sensors. Algal fouling that produce or consume oxygen, however, might inmpact measurements. 
:::

<!-- Link factor user manual -->
- Inspect the foil for any serious damage, including tears or large scratches. Damaged foil may be replaced in accordance with the procedures outlined in the factory user manual.


### Storage

- Place a wet piece of natural sponge in the black rubber protection cap and reinstall over the optode to keep the sensor foil wet and shielded from ambient light at all times during storage.

### Pre-deployment

- Ensure the natural sponge is wet and in place. If not, put in place to keep the sensor wetted at least 48 hours prior to deploymet. 

- Peform a functional test of the optode. Oxygen saturation should be near 100% in air at sea level and decrease when breathing on the foil. Temperature should reflect the ambient room temperature. 

### Annual Recalibration

- It is optimal and recommended that the optode is recalibrated annually.

## Salinity and Depth Compensation

### Salinity

<!--NOTE not sure how we are currently handling this? Fluctuation about 1ppt in the California Current? And probably more variable for the AMLR gliders? Salinity correction could be applied post-collection during data processing step?-->
::: {.callout-important}

:::

From manual - "Aanderaa Optodes are measuring the level of oxygen saturation (partial pressure) in the water and not the absolute concentrations. To get the absolute concentrations, the salinity has to be measured in parallel/known and compensated for. This can be done either internally by setting the salinity to a fixed value or externally by applying the formulas suggested by Garcia and Gordon (1992)."

### Depth

<!--NOTE Also not sure how we are handling this? Not sure if it's significant enough unless caring about 0-1000dbar profile range when we dive deep? Science off < 500m? Depth correction could be applied during data processing step?-->

<!-- NOTE less than .01 mg/L change for low oxygen measurements at depth-->

The response of the sensing foil decreases with increased ambient water pressure. 

::: {.callout-important}
Depth compensation is not performed within the Optode and must be handled during data processing.
:::

The depth-compensated O$_2$ concentration, O$_{2c}$, is calculated 
from the following equation:

$$
O_{2c} = O_2 \cdot \left(1 + 0.032 \cdot \frac{d}{1000}\right)
$$

where:

- $d$ is depth in meters or pressure in dbar.
- $O_2$ is the measured O$_2$ concentration in either $\mu$M or %.
